title: Risk-Informed Nature-Based Coastal Adaptation Under Climate Change: Evidence from a Sheltered Black Sea Embayment
content: Nature-based solutions (NbS) offer coastal adaptation benefits, yet evaluating individual measures does not establish whether their combinations form robust adaptation pathways. This study develops a risk-informed framework for Foros Bay, a sheltered Black Sea embayment, combining Delft3D-FM–XBeach simulations of seagrass responses under climate-change scenarios, parameter-derived sediment organic carbon burial estimates, and multi-criteria assessment of three adaptation pathways: Coastal Protection, Restoring Connectivity and Nature Restoration. Pathway-level trade-off penalties account for potential integration constraints, while sensitivity analyses examine ranking robustness under alternative weights, expert-assigned scores and penalty classifications. Relative to unvegetated conditions, existing seagrass reduced modelled erosion volume and extent by averages of 71.6% and 58.4%, respectively. Inundated area decreased by approximately 7% on average, primarily where sediment stabilisation limited coastal barrier breaching. Expanding modelled seagrass coverage from 40 to 90 ha provided greater additional reductions in erosion extent than inundation. The estimated mature gross sediment organic carbon-burial capacity of the 90 ha meadow was 14.26 Mg C yr⁻¹. Restoring Connectivity ranked first in all baseline scenarios and 82.4–84.6% of deterministic combined score-and-penalty configurations. Nature Restoration retained substantial ecosystem-service potential, while Coastal Protection provided targeted buffering. By distinguishing modelled physical effects from expert-informed pathway evaluation, the framework connects between-measure trade-offs and ranking robustness to adaptive coastal design.
